rv.q: “Birthday Candles” is even better.
Metcalf's performance is nothing short of extraordinary, finding fresh colors in what could have been a repetitive exercise.
Not even a tacked-on final birthday scene that strains credulity can sour the simple, icing-sweet pleasures of Birthday Candles.
This play feels like an offering, a true gift, a lesson on survival and a bold reminder to live each day with zest and adventure.
Messing, meanwhile, doesn’t quite rise to the occasion of her one very challenging part.
Too much rests on Messing’s shoulders, and it’s simply the wrong play for her gifts.
Birthday Candles isn’t interested in characters, and as it skips forward through the years it doesn’t have much time to develop them.
Instead, this Roundabout Theater Company production gets caught in a superficial cycle of wannabe profundities and emotional pantomimes.
Because what begins sweetly enough only grows treacly and saccharin the longer it lingers on the palate.

One could have a cynical reaction to “Birthday Candles,” finding it sentimental and manipulative, with existential queries and lines of “King Lear” that are didactically repeated in an attempt to make it seem profound.
While the play often feels half-baked, the gifted thespians onstage make traveling the circuitous path of “Birthday Candles” seem like a piece of cake!
Neither has “Birthday Candles.”
As it confronts the big and small questions of existence and time itself, Birthday Candles itself proves simultaneously over-baked and under-baked, but its performers ensure it is served warm.
It's hard not to wish Haidle had used that time to adjust some of the play's ingredients.
Debra Messing generally has too little to work with, only coming into her own as Ernestine herself comes into her own.
For all the baking going on, however, Birthday Candles remains stubbornly half-baked.
There might be life beyond the walls of Ernestine’s expansive Grand Rapids, Michigan, kitchen, but Birthday Candles isn’t interested in it.
The play fails to deliver anything of greater substance — it is just dessert, all sugar.
Generic characters whose paths resemble some universal cycle of life fall flat because there is nothing about them that’s even remotely interesting.

Birthday Candles should have felt close to home and pulled on my heartstrings, but instead it just felt like a disappointing bite of bland cake overcompensating with achingly sweet buttercream frosting.
With “Birthday Candles,” it’s more like Wilder overdosing on Sweet ‘N Low.
Birthday Candles is an expositional attempt to reconcile humanity’s smallness with the universe’s grandness.
Unfortunately, she does not make the connection.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this life-spanning drama, with some finding warmth and poignancy in Messing's performance, while others dismiss it as manipulative, clichéd fluff that mistakes simple observations for profound insight.
